p.src: The tale tells how the Tang Monk and his three disciples left Yuhua City and journeyed on in peace, through what truly might be called a land of perfect bliss. After five or six days on the road, they saw another walled city. The Tang Monk asked the Pilgrim, “What place is this?” The Pilgrim replied, “It is a walled city. But there is a flagstaff on the wall with no flag flying, so I cannot tell what place it is. We shall ask when we draw nearer.” When they reached the eastern suburbs, they found the teahouses and wine shops on either side bustling with noise, while the rice market and oil mills thronged with activity. Several idle young loafers in the streets saw Zhu Bajie’s long snout, Friar Sand’s black face, and Sun the Pilgrim’s red eyes. They crowded round, jostling one another for a look, though none dared approach and question them. The Tang Monk’s palms grew clammy with fear that his disciples might cause trouble. They passed several more alleyways but still had not reached the inner city. Suddenly they saw the gate of a monastery, above which were written the three characters “Ciyun Temple.” The Tang Monk said, “What do you say to going in for a short rest, to give the horse a respite and ask for a vegetarian meal?” “Good, good,” replied the Pilgrim. So all four entered together. Inside they saw:

p.src: As the four were looking about, a monk came out from beneath the gallery, bowed to the Tang Monk, and asked, “Reverend sir, whence have you come?” The Tang Monk replied, “Your disciple comes from the Tang court in the Middle Kingdom.” At this, the monk prostrated himself. Startled, the Tang Monk helped him up and said, “Why does the master of this monastery show me such great homage?” With palms joined, the monk said, “The devout people here who study the sutras and invoke the Buddha all hope that through cultivation they may be reborn in your Middle Kingdom. When I beheld your noble bearing and attire, reverend sir, I knew that only merit cultivated in a former life could have won such blessings; therefore I bowed before you.” The Tang Monk smiled. “You overwhelm me; you overwhelm me. I am but a wandering mendicant. What comforts do I enjoy? It is you, living here at ease and free from care, who truly enjoy good fortune.” The monk led the Tang Monk into the main hall. After he had paid homage to the image of the Buddha, the Tang Monk called his disciples inside. It happened that when the three disciples saw the monk speaking with their master, they had turned their faces away and stood together, one holding the horse and another guarding the luggage; thus the monk had paid them no attention. Only when they suddenly heard the Tang Monk call “Disciples!” did all three turn around. At the sight of them, the monk cried out in alarm, “Merciful heavens! How have your distinguished disciples come to look so hideous?” The Tang Monk replied, “Ugly they may be, but they possess considerable magic powers. Throughout my journey I have owed much to their protection.”

p.src: While they were speaking, several more monks came out from within and bowed in greeting. The monk who had first appeared told the newcomers, “This reverend gentleman comes from the Great Tang in the Middle Kingdom, and those three are his distinguished disciples.” Both delighted and fearful, the monks asked, “Reverend sir, what brings you here from the great realm of the Middle Kingdom?” The Tang Monk said, “By sacred command of the Tang emperor, I am journeying to Vulture Peak to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. As I happened to pass through your honored region, I came especially to this noble monastery, first to inquire about the country and second to take a vegetarian meal before continuing on my way.” Every one of the monks was delighted, and they invited the travelers into the abbot’s quarters. Several monks were already there preparing a religious meal for lay patrons. The monks who entered first called to them, “Come and see these people from the Middle Kingdom! It turns out that in the Middle Kingdom there are both handsome people and ugly ones. The handsome one is truly beyond painting or description, while the ugly ones are exceedingly strange.” The many monks and the patrons of the meal all came forward to meet them. When the introductions were over, everyone sat down. After tea, the Tang Monk asked, “What is the name of this place?” The monks replied, “This is Jinping Prefecture, an outlying commandery of the Kingdom of India.” The Tang Monk asked, “How far is it from your prefecture to Vulture Peak?” The monks replied, “From here to the capital is two thousand li. That road we ourselves have traveled. But we have never journeyed westward to Vulture Peak, so we do not know how much farther it may be and dare not answer rashly.” The Tang Monk thanked them.

p.src: Before long, the vegetarian meal was served. When the meal was over, the Tang Monk wished to leave, but the monks and their patrons pressed him to stay, saying, “Reverend sir, remain at ease for a day or two. There will be no harm in enjoying the Lantern Festival before you go.” Surprised, the Tang Monk asked, “On the road I have thought only of the mountains and rivers, fearing that some monster or demon might waylay us and waste all our time. I have lost track of the days—when is the Lantern Festival?” The monks laughed. “Reverend sir, your heart is so intent on worshiping the Buddha and awakening to Chan that you give no thought to such things. Today is the thirteenth day of the first month, and the lanterns will be tried this evening. The day after tomorrow, the fifteenth, is the Upper Prime Festival. The lanterns are not taken down until the eighteenth or nineteenth. The people here delight in festivities, and the prefect, who loves his people, has tall lantern displays erected everywhere while reed pipes and flutes sound throughout the night. There is also a Golden Lantern Bridge, handed down from ancient times, whose festivities flourish to this day. Good sirs, stay for several days. Though ours is but a remote mountain temple, we can well afford to entertain you.” Unable to refuse, the Tang Monk and his disciples all stayed. That evening the bells and drums in the Buddha hall thundered to the heavens: the faithful from the neighborhood had come to offer lanterns to the Buddha. The Tang Monk and the others came out from the abbot’s quarters to view the lanterns, then each retired to sleep.

p.src: The following day, the Tang Monk said to the monks, “I made a vow long ago to sweep a pagoda. As today is the blessed Upper Prime Festival, I ask the master of the monastery to open the pagoda door and allow me to fulfill my vow.” The monks accordingly opened the door. Friar Sand took the cassock and followed the Tang Monk. On reaching the first story, the Tang Monk donned the cassock, bowed to the Buddha, and finished his prayers. He then swept that story with a broom, removed the cassock, and handed it to Friar Sand. …Then he swept the second story, and continued story by story until he reached the very top. Every story of the pagoda housed a Buddha, and windows opened everywhere. As he swept each story, he admired it and voiced his praise. By the time he finished sweeping and descended, evening had fallen and all the lanterns had again been lit.

p.src: When they reached the Golden-Lamp Bridge, Tripitaka and the monks went forward to look and saw that there were indeed three golden lamps. Each lamp was as large as a vat, with a two-storeyed pavilion of exquisite openwork rising above it. They were woven entirely of fine gold wire and lined within with thin sheets of glass; their radiance outshone the moon, and their oil gave off a rich fragrance. Tripitaka turned and asked the monks, “What kind of oil is used in these lamps? Why does it give off such an extraordinary fragrance?” The monks replied, “Reverend Master, you do not know. Beyond our prefecture lies a county called Mintian, which extends for two hundred and forty li. Every year, when labor levies are assessed, two hundred and forty wealthy households are assigned to provide lamp oil. The other prefectural and county levies are bearable, but these wealthy households suffer greatly: each must spend over two hundred taels of silver during its year of duty. This is no ordinary oil, but fragrant storax oil. Each ounce of it costs two taels of silver, and each catty costs thirty-two taels. There are three lamps, each vat holding five hundred catties; the three vats hold fifteen hundred catties altogether, costing forty-eight thousand taels of silver. With miscellaneous expenses added, the total comes to more than fifty thousand taels—and it lasts for only three nights.” Pilgrim said, “With so much oil, how can it possibly be burned up in three nights?” The monks replied, “In each vat there are forty-nine great wicks, made from bundles of rush pith wrapped in floss silk, each as thick as a hen’s egg. Once they have burned through tonight and the Buddhas have manifested themselves, by tomorrow night the oil will be gone and the lamps will grow dim.” Bajie laughed beside them and said, “I suppose the Buddhas take the oil away with them.” The monks said, “Exactly so. From ancient times to the present, every household in the city has passed down that very account. Whenever the oil is exhausted, everyone says the Buddha Patriarch has accepted the lamps, and the five grains are sure to yield an abundant harvest. But if in any year it is not exhausted, the year brings drought and poor harvests, and wind and rain come out of season. That is why every household insists on making this offering.”

p.src: As they were speaking, a roaring wind suddenly sounded in midair, frightening all the lamp-watchers into scattering in every direction. The monks, unable to keep their footing, also said, “Reverend Master, let us go back. The wind has come. The Buddhas are descending with their blessing to view the lamps.” Tripitaka asked, “How do you know that the Buddhas are coming to view the lamps?” The monks replied, “It happens this way every year: before the third watch, the wind always rises. We know that the Buddhas are descending with their blessing, and so everyone withdraws.” Tripitaka said, “I am one who thinks upon the Buddha, invokes the Buddha, and worships the Buddha. On this splendid occasion, if the Buddhas truly descend, how blessed it would be to worship them here.” Though the monks repeatedly urged him, they could not persuade him to return. Before long, three figures of Buddhas actually appeared in the wind and approached the lamps. In his excitement, Tripitaka ran to the top of the bridge and prostrated himself. Pilgrim hurriedly pulled him up, saying, “Master, they are no good beings. They must be fiends.” Before he had finished speaking, the lamplight dimmed; with a whoosh, they snatched up Tripitaka and rode the wind away. Alas! Who could know from what mountain and cave these true monsters had come, year after year posing as Buddhas to view the golden lamps? Bajie was so alarmed that he searched on both sides, while Friar Sand called out in every direction. Pilgrim called, “Brothers, there is no need to shout here. At the height of joy, sorrow has befallen Master; the fiends have already carried him off.” The frightened monks asked, “Grandfather, how do you know that fiends carried him off?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “So you mortals have failed to recognize them all these years and have been deluded by evil spirits, believing that true Buddhas descended with blessings to receive these offerings of lamplight. Those who appeared as Buddhas when the wind rose just now were three fiends. My master could not recognize them either. He went to the top of the bridge and bowed, whereupon they darkened the lamplight, filled vessels with the oil, and carried off my master as well. I was only a little too slow in pursuing them, and so the three transformed themselves into wind and escaped.” Friar Sand said, “Elder Brother, what are we to do now?” Pilgrim replied, “There is no time to hesitate. You two return to the monastery with the others and guard the horse and luggage, while old Monkey follows this wind in pursuit.”

p.src: As the Great Sage searched for a path along the cliff, he saw four men driving three sheep down the western slope, all shouting together, “Open the way to prosperity!” The Great Sage flashed his fiery eyes and golden pupils and looked closely. He recognized the four as the Duty Gods of the Year, Month, Day, and Hour, who had come in disguised forms. The Great Sage at once drew out his iron staff and gave it a shake, making it as thick as a rice bowl and twelve feet long. Leaping down from the cliff, he shouted, “Where do you think you are going, skulking with your heads hidden and necks drawn in?” When the four Duty Gods heard that he had seen through their ruse, they hurriedly scattered the three sheep, resumed their true forms, stepped to the roadside, and bowed, saying, “Great Sage, forgive us! Forgive us!” Pilgrim said, “I have had no occasion to call upon you lately, and because old Monkey has been indulgent, every one of you has grown slack. You do not even come to pay your respects—what do you mean by this? Why were you not secretly protecting my master? Where have you all been?” The Duty Gods replied, “Your master relaxed his meditative discipline and lingered in pleasure at Ciyun Monastery in Jinping Prefecture. Thus, after prosperity came adversity, and at the height of joy sorrow arose; now he has been captured by fiends. The guardian deities of the Dharma are protecting him at his side. We knew that the Great Sage had been searching all night and feared that you might not know these mountains and forests, so we came especially to inform you.” Pilgrim said, “If you came to inform me, why did you hide your identities, drive three sheep along, and shout at them so?” The Duty Gods replied, “We arranged these three sheep to answer the phrase ‘opening prosperity.’ It is called ‘Three Yang Open Prosperity,’ and is meant to break your master’s present adversity and obstruction.” Pilgrim angrily raised his staff to strike them, but seeing that they meant well, he spared them. Putting away his staff, he turned from anger to delight and asked, “Is this mountain the fiends’ lair?” The Duty Gods replied, “It is, it is. This mountain is called Green Dragon Mountain, and within it is a cave called Dark Blossom Cave. Three fiends dwell in the cave: the eldest is called Great King Cold-Dispeller, the second Great King Heat-Dispeller, and the third Great King Dust-Dispeller. These fiends have been here for a thousand years. Since childhood they have loved to consume fragrant storax oil. After becoming spirits, they came here and disguised themselves as Buddhas, deceiving the officials and people of Jinping Prefecture into erecting golden lamps fueled with fragrant storax oil. Every year on the fifteenth day of the first month, they transform into Buddhas and come to collect the oil. This year they saw your master and recognized him as a holy monk, so they carried him into their cave as well. Before long they intend to carve up his flesh, fry it in fragrant storax oil, and eat it. Quickly use your powers and go to his rescue.”

Pilgrim angrily raised his staff to strike them, but seeing that they meant well, he spared them. Putting away his staff, he turned from anger to delight and asked, “Is this mountain the fiends’ lair?”
The Duty Gods replied, “It is, it is.
This mountain is called Green Dragon Mountain, and within it is a cave called Dark Blossom Cave.
Three fiends dwell in the cave: the eldest is called Great King Cold-Dispeller, the second Great King Heat-Dispeller, and the third Great King Dust-Dispeller.
These fiends have been here for a thousand years.

Since childhood they have loved to consume fragrant storax oil. After becoming spirits, they came here and disguised themselves as Buddhas, deceiving the officials and people of Jinping Prefecture into erecting golden lamps fueled with fragrant storax oil.

u.src: Every year on the fifteenth day of the first month, they transform into Buddhas and come to collect the oil.

This year they saw your master and recognized him as a holy monk, so they carried him into their cave as well. Before long they intend to carve up his flesh, fry it in fragrant storax oil, and eat it.
Quickly use your powers and go to his rescue.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim shouted for the Four Merit Officers to withdraw, then rounded the mountain cliff in search of the cave dwelling. After going only a few li, he saw a rocky cliff beside the ravine. Beneath the cliff stood a stone house with two stone doors, left half open and half closed. Beside the doors stood a stone tablet bearing six characters: “Mystic Hero Cave, Azure Dragon Mountain.” The Pilgrim dared not enter unbidden. Halting in his tracks, he called, “Monsters! Send my master out at once!” With a sudden clatter, the doors flew wide open, and a troop of ox-headed fiends rushed out. Staring stupidly, they demanded, “Who are you, to dare shout here?” The Pilgrim said, “I am the chief disciple of Tang Sanzang, the holy monk journeying from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch the scriptures. While passing through Jinping Prefecture to view the lanterns, my master was abducted by your demon lords. Return him quickly, and I shall spare your lives; otherwise, I shall overturn your lair and reduce every fiend among you to blood and pus!”

p.src: At these words, the lesser demons hurried inside to report, “Disaster, Great Kings! Disaster!” The three old demons had taken the Tang Monk deep into the cave. Without troubling to ask right from wrong, they had ordered their underlings to strip off his clothes, draw clear water from the rushing stream to wash him clean, and were planning to slice and mince him finely, then fry him in fragrant clarified butter and oil to eat. Suddenly hearing the cry of “Disaster,” the eldest demon was startled and asked what had happened. A lesser demon said, “Before the main gate is a monk with a hairy face and a thunder-god’s snout. He is shouting that the Great Kings abducted his master and must send him out at once if our lives are to be spared; otherwise, he will overturn our lair and reduce us all to blood and pus.” When the old demons heard this, each of them was alarmed. “We have only just captured this fellow and have not yet asked his name or origins. Underlings, put his clothes back on him for now and bring him here for questioning, so that we may discover who he truly is and whence he came.”

p.src: The demons surged forward together, untied the Tang Monk’s ropes, dressed him, and shoved him before the thrones. Terrified, the Tang Monk knelt below, trembling all over, and cried only, “Spare my life, Great Kings! Spare my life!” The three demons asked in one voice, “From what region do you come, monk? Why did you not keep out of the way when you saw the forms of Buddhas, but instead obstructed our path through the clouds?” The Tang Monk kowtowed and said, “This poor monk was dispatched by the sovereign of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to worship the Buddha and fetch scriptures from the Great Thunderclap Monastery in the land of India. When I reached Ciyun Monastery in Jinping Prefecture to receive alms, its monks persuaded me to remain for the Lantern Festival and view the lanterns. While I was on Golden Lantern Bridge, I saw Your Majesties manifest the forms of Buddhas. Being but mortal flesh with mortal eyes, I bowed when I saw Buddhas, and thus inadvertently obstructed Your Majesties’ path through the clouds.” The demons said, “The journey from your Eastern Land to this place is exceedingly long. How many are there in your company altogether? What are all their names? Confess the truth at once, and I shall spare your life.” The Tang Monk said, “My secular name is Chen Xuanzang, and I became a monk at Golden Mountain Monastery in my childhood. Later, by imperial decree of the Tang emperor, I was appointed a clerical official at Hongfu Monastery in Chang’an. Then, because Prime Minister Wei Zheng beheaded the old dragon of the Jing River in a dream, the Tang emperor journeyed through the underworld and, after returning to life in the mortal realm, convened a Grand Mass of Land and Water to deliver the departed souls. The Tang emperor chose this poor monk to preside over the altar and serve as chief officiant in expounding the Dharma. By good fortune, the Bodhisattva Guanyin appeared and enlightened this poor monk, saying that the Great Thunderclap Monastery in the Western Heaven possessed the true scriptures of the Tripitaka, which could deliver the dead to Heaven. She sent me to fetch them, and so I was granted the religious name Tripitaka. Since I took Tang as my surname, everyone calls me Tang Sanzang. I have three disciples. The first is surnamed Sun and named Wukong, the Pilgrim; he is the Great Sage Equaling Heaven, now returned to the true path.” At this name, all the demons started in alarm and asked, “Is this Great Sage Equaling Heaven the one who caused havoc in Heaven five hundred years ago?” The Tang Monk said, “The very same, the very same. The second is surnamed Zhu and named Wuneng, or Bajie; he is the reincarnation of the Great Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds. The third is surnamed Sha and named Wujing, a monk; he is the Curtain-Raising General descended to the mortal world.”

Each took up a weapon and marched out through the gate, where they sounded their signals, waved their banners, and beat their drums. The three demons, fully armed and accoutred, came outside and shouted, “Who dares make a clamor in our domain?” The Pilgrim slipped onto the rocky cliff and looked carefully. p.src: After watching for a while, Pilgrim Sun could restrain himself no longer. He stepped forward and shouted, “You accursed thieving monsters! Do you recognize old Sun?” The demons shouted, “Are you Sun Wukong, who caused havoc in Heaven? We had indeed heard your name without ever seeing you, but the sight of you would put the gods themselves to shame. So you are nothing more than such a scrawny little monkey!” The Pilgrim flew into a rage and cursed, “You lamp-oil-stealing thieves, you oily-mouthed monsters! Enough of your nonsense—return my master at once!” He rushed forward and swung his iron staff to strike; the three old demons raised their three different weapons and hurriedly parried his blow. What a fierce battle they fought in that mountain hollow:

p.src: With his single staff, Pilgrim Sun fought the three demons for a hundred and fifty rounds. Evening drew near, yet neither side had gained the victory. Then Great King Dust-Dispeller brandished his rattan cudgel, leapt beyond the battle line, and waved the banner once. The horde of ox-headed monsters surged forward and surrounded the Pilgrim in the very center. Each swung his weapon and struck at him wildly. Seeing that matters had turned against him, the Pilgrim sprang up with a whoosh onto his somersault cloud and fled in defeat. The demons did not pursue him. They called their horde back, prepared an evening meal, and all ate their fill. They also ordered a lesser demon to take a bowl to the Tang Monk, intending to deal with him only after Sun Wukong and the others had been captured. But the master, being both a lifelong vegetarian and overwhelmed by grief, merely wept and dared not let the food touch his lips. Of this, no more need be said.

p.src: Now Sun Wukong rode his cloud back to Ciyun Monastery and called out, “Brothers!” Bajie and Sha Wujing had been anxiously waiting and discussing matters. When they heard his call, they came out together to meet him and said, “Brother, why have you been gone all day before returning? What, exactly, has become of Master?” Wukong laughed and said, “Last night I followed the wind in pursuit until dawn, when I reached a mountain but found no trace of him. Fortunately, the Four Duty Gods brought word that the mountain is called Green Dragon Mountain and that there is a Xuanying Cave within it. Three demons dwell in the cave, called the Great King Warder of Cold, the Great King Warder of Heat, and the Great King Warder of Dust. For years they have been stealing the lamp oil here, disguising themselves as Buddha images and deceiving the officials and people of Jinping Prefecture. This year they encountered us, and, unable to tell good from ill, went so far as to abduct Master too. Once I had learned the truth, I ordered the Duty Gods and the others to protect Master in secret, while I went near the cave entrance and hurled challenges and abuse. All three monsters came out, each looking like an ox-headed demon. The first wielded a battle-axe, the second a great saber, and the third a rattan staff. Behind them came a whole brood of ox-headed fiends, waving banners and beating drums. They fought me all day, and neither side gained the upper hand. Whenever the demon kings waved their banners, all the lesser demons swarmed forward. When I saw night falling, I feared I could not win, so I turned a somersault and came back.” Bajie said, “Could it be the ghost kings of Fengdu raising a commotion there?” Sha Wujing said, “How did you come to guess that it was the ghost kings of Fengdu raising a commotion?” Bajie laughed and said, “Brother said they were ox-headed fiends, so naturally I knew.” Wukong said, “No, no. Judging by what I saw, those monsters are spirits formed from three rhinoceroses.” Bajie said, “If they are rhinoceroses, let us capture them and saw off their horns. Those would fetch a fair few taels of silver!”

p.src: As they were speaking, the monks asked, “Would Lord Sun care to eat the evening meal?” Wukong replied, “If it is convenient, I will eat a little; if not, never mind.” The monks said, “After fighting all day, my lord, can you not be hungry?” Wukong laughed and said, “How could a mere day leave me hungry? I once went five hundred years without food or drink.” The monks did not know this was true and took it merely as a jest. Presently the food was brought, and Wukong ate as well. Then he said, “Let us put things in order and sleep. Tomorrow we shall all go and confront them. If we capture the demon kings, we should be able to rescue Master.” Sha Wujing, standing beside him, said, “Brother, what are you saying? As the saying goes, ‘Delay breeds wisdom.’ What if those demons remain awake tonight and harm Master? What would we do then? Better to go at once and raise such an uproar that they are caught unprepared; only then can we readily rescue Master. If we delay even a little, I fear something may go wrong.” Hearing this, Bajie roused his martial spirit and said, “Brother Sha is right. Let us all take advantage of the moonlight and go subdue the demons.” Wukong agreed and immediately instructed the temple monks, “Guard our luggage and horses. Once we have captured the demons, we shall bring them before the prefect of this prefecture and prove that they were false Buddhas. Then the levy of lamp oil can be abolished and the hardship of the common people throughout the county relieved. Would that not be a good thing?” The monks obeyed. The three disciples then mounted auspicious clouds and departed from the city. And so it was that:
